an0333.user: Need a sanity check on my Google Search numbers, last 30 days for my snacks brand. AOV ₹2,850, gross margin 51%, CAC ₹878, ROAS 3.2, CTR 1.5%. 90-day repeat sits at 10%. ROAS looks healthy to me but something feels off. What's wrong?
an0333.assistant:
Your acquisition is genuinely good — that's not the problem. First-order contribution is ₹2,850 × 51% − ₹878 = +₹576 per order, and a 3.2 ROAS backs that up. If this were the whole story I'd tell you to pour fuel on it.

The problem is the line you mentioned almost as an afterthought: 90-day repeat at 10%. For a snacks brand that number should scare you. Snacks are the most repeat-friendly category there is — people finish a pack and reorder if they liked it. 10% repeat means 9 out of 10 buyers try you once and vanish. So every rupee of LTV you have is basically that single +₹576, and then the bucket empties.

The mechanism isn't ads, it's retention. You've built a machine that's excellent at finding first-time buyers and terrible at keeping them. Scaling spend right now just pours more water into a bucket with no bottom — you'll grow revenue and shrink your margin of safety at the same time.

Fix repeat before you touch the budget. Set up a WhatsApp/email reorder flow at day 20-25 with a returning-customer offer, and look hard at whether the product itself is good enough to want again. One caveat: 90-day repeat on a snack should really be read on a longer tail, so pull the 180-day cohort too — but even being generous, 10% is a leak, not a rounding error.

an0334.user: Quick one — why is my CTR low? Running WhatsApp broadcasts for my no-code SaaS, CTR is 1.9%. Last 30 days the funnel was 48,000 visits, 3,713 add to cart, 2,260 reached checkout, 544 purchases. Trying to figure out where to push.
an0334.assistant:
Forget CTR — 1.9% is fine and it's not where your money is leaking. Walk the funnel and the problem jumps out.

48,000 visits to 3,713 add-to-cart is an 8% ATC rate — healthy. 3,713 down to 2,260 reaching checkout is normal drop-off. Then 2,260 reached checkout but only 544 bought. That's a 24% checkout-to-purchase rate. People who reach a checkout page have already decided to buy; that number should sit around 50-70%. Yours is less than half of where it should be.

The leak is the very last step, not acquisition. Something at payment is killing intent: surprise shipping cost revealed only at checkout, a forced account/login wall, a clunky payment step, or missing UPI/COD options that Indian buyers expect. You're losing roughly 1,200 people who were standing at the till with their wallet out.

Don't touch the ads or the broadcast creative — that side is working. Instrument the checkout: watch session recordings of abandoned checkouts and add UPI plus COD if they're missing. Recovering even half of that drop-off would more than double your orders off the exact same traffic. The one number to confirm first: where exactly in the checkout the field drop happens — that tells you whether it's cost-shock or a friction wall.

an0335.user: Looking for a non-obvious read here. Google Search, apparel, last 6 weeks. AOV ₹1,200, margin 56%. CAC has gone from ₹562 to ₹1,122, ROAS from 2.1 down to 1.1. Frequency is 2.7. CTR is sliding. I haven't changed creatives or audience. Don't think it's the obvious targeting story.
an0335.assistant:
You're right that it's not targeting — and the fact that you've held creatives and audience constant is exactly the tell.

Do the contribution math at today's CAC: ₹1,200 × 56% − ₹1,122 = −₹450 per order. Six weeks ago at ₹562 CAC you were comfortably positive; now every order loses you ₹450. So this isn't a slow drift, it's a real reversal.

The mechanism is creative fatigue, and the numbers spell it cleanly. CAC nearly doubled, ROAS halved, CTR sliding — all while frequency climbed to 2.7. Above ~2.5 your audience is seeing the same ads often enough to tune them out. Same creative, same people, more exposure: response decays, the auction makes you pay more for each click, CAC rises. The algorithm isn't broken and your targeting didn't rot; your ads just got old.

The lever is creative, not budget or bids. Ship 3-4 genuinely new angles — different hook, different problem, different format — and rebuild a testing cadence so you're never riding a single winner to exhaustion again. That cadence is the real fix; the refresh is just the patch.

One honest caveat: six weeks of one channel can also catch a seasonal lull in apparel search demand, so glance at your category's search trend before you conclude. But fatigue at frequency 2.7 with frozen creative is the far likelier story.

an0336.user: Coffee brand, comparing channels and email jumped out — conversion rate dropped 8% this week vs last week. That's on 112 conversions. I'm ready to overhaul the whole email strategy. Where do I start?
an0336.assistant:
Start by doing nothing. Seriously.

An 8% move in conversion rate on 112 conversions is noise, not a trend. At that sample size the week-to-week wobble from pure randomness is easily bigger than 8% — a handful of buyers landing on one side of the week instead of the other moves the number by that much. You're about to rebuild a strategy on top of a coin-flip.

This is the single most expensive habit a founder can have: reacting to one noisy week, changing things, then reacting to the next noisy week the change happened to coincide with, and whipsawing the account into the ground.

What would actually count as a signal: the same direction holding for 3-4 weeks in a row, or a single move big enough to clearly clear the noise band on this volume. Until then, leave the email program exactly as it is and look at it again at month-end. If you're itching to act, spend that energy growing the sample — get the volume up so next month's numbers are actually readable.

an0337.user: Why's my CTR weak on YouTube? Apparel label, last 8 weeks. I scaled spend from ₹6.5L to ₹12.9L. AOV ₹1,050, margin 65%. CAC went ₹404 to ₹676, ROAS 2.6 down to 1.6. Feels like the ads are getting worse.
an0337.assistant:
CTR is a distraction here — the story is in what happened the moment you doubled spend.

You took budget from ₹6.5L to ₹12.9L, and right alongside it CAC climbed ₹404 → ₹676 and ROAS fell 2.6 → 1.6. That's not the ads getting worse; that's the channel telling you it has a ceiling and you've hit it. Your first ₹6.5L bought your best, highest-intent viewers. The extra ₹6.4L is buying progressively colder, pricier reach — the same finite pool, dredged deeper.

Contribution still survives: ₹1,050 × 65% − ₹676 = +₹6.5 per order. You haven't gone underwater, but you've spent ₹6.4L of extra budget to push contribution to roughly break-even. That's the wall — more money is buying worse efficiency, not more good customers.

The lever isn't another budget bump; it's new demand. New audiences, new creative angles, or a new channel to open a fresh pool before you add spend. Pouring more into a saturated set just keeps bidding up the same exhausted inventory.

Caveat: confirm the spend ramp was steady and not lumpy week-to-week, and that no festive period inflated CAC mid-window — but the clean inverse march of spend up, ROAS down is a textbook saturation curve.

an0338.user: Logistics SaaS, YouTube. Why does my CTR look off — my ROAS just dropped 11% this week compared to last. That's on 99 conversions for the week. I'm thinking of reworking the entire campaign structure. Thoughts?
an0338.assistant:
Don't rework anything yet — there's no signal here to act on.

An 11% ROAS swing on 99 conversions is well inside normal week-to-week variance. At ~100 conversions the random noise band alone is wider than 11%; a few deals slipping from one week into the next moves ROAS by more than that without anything actually changing. You'd be redesigning your campaigns based on a dice roll.

That's exactly how accounts get whipsawed — overhaul this week, the next noisy week swings the other way, you blame or credit the change, and you're permanently chasing your own tail instead of letting the account stabilise and learn.

What would make this real: the ROAS decline holding the same direction for 3-4 consecutive weeks, or a single drop large enough to obviously break out of the noise on this volume. Until one of those shows up, leave the campaign structure alone and re-read it at month-end on the fuller sample. One week is weather, not climate.

an0339.user: Eyewear brand, just started running Meesho Ads. Over the last 4 days I've spent about ₹30K and gotten 21 conversions. Is my CAC good? Should I scale this or kill it?
an0339.assistant:

21 conversions over 4 days is far too thin to conclude anything. Scaling on it risks pouring budget into something that only looked good for four lucky days; killing it risks throwing away something that was actually fine. Both decisions would be guesses dressed up as data.

Don't make either call now. Let it run untouched until you've got roughly 100 conversions or a clean 2-3 week window — whichever comes first. That's the threshold where the CAC stops bouncing and starts meaning something. Check back then with the same numbers and we'll have a real read. Right now there's nothing to diagnose.

an0340.user: Meesho Ads for my eyewear brand — why is my CTR low? Over 8 weeks I took spend from ₹3.5L to ₹7.1L. AOV ₹1,850, margin 45%. CAC went ₹371 to ₹604, ROAS dropped from 5.0 to 3.1. Want to keep scaling but it's getting harder.

CTR isn't your issue — the pattern in your scaling numbers is, and it's a good problem to have hit.

You doubled spend from ₹3.5L to ₹7.1L, and ROAS fell 5.0 → 3.1 while CAC climbed ₹371 → ₹604. That inverse move — more budget, lower efficiency — is the signature of a channel hitting its ceiling. Your early spend reached the cheapest, most ready-to-buy Meesho shoppers. The extra ₹3.6L is reaching colder buyers in the same pool, so each order costs more.

The good news: you're still well in the black. Contribution = ₹1,850 × 45% − ₹604 = +₹228 per order. At ROAS 3.1 this isn't broken, it's maturing — it just won't keep absorbing budget at 5.0 efficiency, because that efficiency lived in a finite pool you've now largely drained.

So the lever isn't 'scale harder on Meesho' — it's open new demand. Fresh creative angles, new audience segments, or a second channel, so you're acquiring from a new pool instead of overpaying for the last drops of this one. Keep this channel running at its profitable level; just stop expecting it to scale infinitely.

an0341.user: Haircare brand here. I run WhatsApp broadcasts and the last 30 days look solid — AOV around ₹1,050, margin 45%, CAC ₹313, ROAS 3.4, CTR 1.3%. an0341.assistant:
Your instinct to scale is reading the wrong number, and the number you flagged as 'low forever' is the one that should stop you.

The front end is genuinely healthy: contribution = ₹1,050 × 45% − ₹313 = +₹160 per order, ROAS 3.4. Acquisition works. But haircare lives or dies on repeat — shampoo, oil, serum, these are consumables people are supposed to rebuy every few weeks. A 9% 90-day repeat means 91 of every 100 buyers never come back. That's not a slow leak, that's the floor falling out.

With repeat this low, your LTV is basically that single +₹160 and nothing after it. You've built a great first-order machine bolted onto a product or experience people don't return to. Scaling spend now just multiplies one-time buyers — you'll grow top-line and keep your safety margin paper-thin.

Fix repeat first. Set up a WhatsApp replenishment nudge timed to when the product runs out (for haircare, roughly the 30-45 day mark), and interrogate why people don't reorder — is it the product, the price, or simply that you never reminded them? One caveat: pull the 180-day cohort too, since some haircare repeat cycles run longer than 90 days. But even generously read, 9% says retention, not budget, is your next move.

an0342.user: My ROAS is trash and I think Meesho's algo is broken for me. Candle brand, ₹13L spend last 30 days, AOV ₹1,750, margin 62%, CAC ₹1,032, ROAS only 1.7, CTR 1.7%, repeat 31%. I'm about to cut this whole channel before it bleeds me dry.

This account isn't a candidate to cut — it's a candidate to scale. The lever is to stop judging it on ROAS and start judging it on contribution per order plus repeat value. As long as contribution stays positive as you spend, push more budget in, not less.

One caveat: contribution at +₹53 is thin, so watch it as you scale — if CAC creeps up and pushes it toward zero, that's your real ceiling. But cutting a +₹53, 31%-repeat channel because ROAS reads 1.7 would be a textbook unforced error.

an0343.user: Candle brand, YouTube. Calm question for you — how do I lower my CAC? Last 30 days: AOV ₹1,350, gross margin 32%, CAC ₹544, ROAS 2.5, CTR 1.9%. The CAC feels high and I want to bring it down before scaling.
an0343.assistant:
You're asking how to lower CAC, but CAC isn't actually what's broken — and chasing it will waste your next three months.

Run the contribution: ₹1,350 × 32% − ₹544 = −₹112 per order. You lose ₹112 on every sale. Now notice where that loss comes from. Your CAC of ₹544 isn't unreasonable for the channel. The killer is the 32% gross margin. After COGS you only keep ₹432 per order to cover a ₹544 acquisition cost — the math is underwater before the ad spend even shows up.

This is a margin problem wearing a marketing costume. Even if a brilliant optimisation shaved CAC from ₹544 to ₹450, you'd still be at −₹18 per order. No targeting tweak, no creative refresh, no bid strategy fixes a 32% margin. The ads aren't the disease.

So the lever isn't lower CAC — it's the margin itself. Pick one: renegotiate COGS (wax, jars, packaging are usually fatter than founders think), raise price or AOV through bundles and sets, or cut a fulfilment cost that's eating the gross. Get the margin from 32% toward the high-40s and the same ₹544 CAC suddenly turns profitable.

Caveat: confirm that 32% is true gross margin after all variable cost — shipping, payment fees, returns. Founders often quote a rosier number, which would make this worse, not better. Either way, fix margin before you touch the ad account.

an0346.user: Eyewear, YouTube, last 30 days. Why is my CTR low? 1.11M impressions, 15,806 clicks, CTR 1.4%. But only 142 orders — conversion rate 0.9%. AOV ₹2,100. I'm running broad-match keywords. Trying to get that CTR up.
an0346.assistant:
Your CTR isn't the problem — chasing it would make things worse. Look one step down the funnel.

1.4% CTR is perfectly normal; 15,806 clicks off 1.11M impressions is plenty of traffic. The number that matters is the 0.9% conversion rate. You're pulling clicks in volume but barely 1 in 100 buys. When CTR is fine and conversion is dead, you're not facing an ad problem — you're facing an intent problem.

The cause is sitting in your setup: broad-match keywords. Broad match casts wide and drags in people researching, comparing, window-shopping 'sunglasses', 'eyewear', 'best glasses' — browsing, not buying. They click because the ad is relevant to their search; they don't convert because they were never in buying mode. If anything, a higher CTR on broad match just means more low-intent clicks burning budget.

The lever is intent, not clicks. Tighten to high-intent, bottom-of-funnel keywords (buying language, brand and product-specific terms), pile on negative keywords to choke off the browse traffic, and stop optimising toward clicks — optimise toward purchases. You'll likely see CTR dip and orders rise, which is exactly the trade you want.

Caveat: 142 orders is a usable but not huge sample, so make the keyword shift and give it a couple of weeks before judging the new conversion rate — and check the search-terms report to see exactly which broad queries are bleeding you.
